summary.one_liner: A curated, comparison-style list of tunneling tools and services that expose local servers or ports to the public internet, spanning open source self-hosted projects, hosted commercial services, and overlay VPN networks.
summary.what_it_does: This is an "awesome" style list rather than a single program, so it links to many tunneling tools with one-line descriptions. Entries are grouped into sections: open source tunnels (with a note on license where stated), commercial or closed source services, overlay networks and advanced tools, and reference blog posts and discussions. Many entries note language, license, and limitations such as unmaintained status or required accounts. The maintainer states the purpose is to track and compare tools for exposing local web servers under a public domain with automatic HTTPS, even behind NAT. The README also gives recommendations, such as Cloudflare Tunnel for most users and Pangolin or frp for self-hosting. It also states inclusion policies, including a 100-GitHub-star minimum for new open source additions and evidence of customers for commercial products.
use_cases: expose a local web server with HTTPS
self-host a tunnel to reach home services
find an SSH-based port forwarding tool
tunnel through NAT without port forwarding
pick a WireGuard or overlay VPN option
notable: Organized into open source, commercial/closed source, and overlay networks sections, each entry with language and license notes
Includes a stated wish list for an ideal tunnel: domain registration, automatic certificates, and a simple GUI
Gives explicit recommendations (Cloudflare Tunnel for most users, Pangolin or frp for self-hosting)
Flags projects that are unmaintained, archived, or whose hosted servers are down
caveats: Entries are one-line opinions and may be outdated; several projects are noted as unmaintained or unavailable
Includes many closed source and paid services alongside open source options
Not a tool itself, so nothing can be installed or run from this repository
